Esto es una simulación de escenarios, no asesoría financiera.

Compound interest is the idea that you earn returns not just on your original money, but also on the returns you’ve already earned. Over time, it can feel like your money is growing a little faster all by itself—like a snowball rolling downhill, getting bigger as it picks up more snow.

Here’s a simple example: If you start with $100 and earn 10% each year, the first year you’d have $110. The second year, that extra $10 also earns 10%, so you’d get $11 in growth, bringing you to $121. Over many years, the boost from those “returns on returns” can add up significantly.

Benjamin Franklin once left a small sum (about £1,000) to the cities of Boston and Philadelphia, with instructions that it be invested for 200 years. Thanks to compound interest, that modest gift eventually grew into millions of dollars for public works. That’s a real-world taste of how patient investing can harness compounding across generations.

If you’d like to play with the numbers yourself, you could compare how $1,000 grows under simple interest versus compound interest over 30 years. That’s a great way to see the difference firsthand.
